title: Spotting Misleading Charts & Axes
description: Learn to identify common tricks that make charts misleading and how to read axes critically.

interactions.prompt: A bar chart shows Company A revenue at $102M and Company B at $100M, but Company A's bar looks 3x taller. What's most likely wrong?

options.text: The y-axis doesn't start at zero
The bars are different colors
The chart is using the wrong type
The data is probably incorrect

interactions.teachingPreamble: One of the most common ways charts mislead is by truncating the y-axis — starting it at a number other than zero. This can make tiny differences look dramatic. For example, a cable news network once showed a bar chart where a 1% change looked like a 50% jump simply by starting the y-axis at 99%.

interactions.prompt: A Shopify dashboard shows monthly orders: Jan 10,200 → Feb 10,800 → Mar 11,050. The line chart's y-axis runs from 10,000 to 11,200. What should you notice first?

options.text: Growth is accelerating rapidly month over month
The narrow y-axis range exaggerates a modest 8% total increase
Orders are essentially flat and not growing
The data is unreliable because the axis is wrong

interactions.prompt: A pie chart in a Nike quarterly report shows 8 product categories. Why might this be a poor chart choice?

options.text: Pie charts can't show percentages
Too many slices make it hard to compare similar-sized segments
Pie charts only work for exactly four categories
Nike's data is too complex for any chart

interactions.teachingPreamble: Pie charts work best with 2–4 categories where differences are obvious. When you have many slices of similar size, the human eye struggles to compare arc lengths accurately. A horizontal bar chart is almost always a better choice for comparing multiple categories — it's why data teams at companies like Google and Amazon default to bar charts in internal dashboards.

interactions.prompt: A chart that uses two different y-axes (dual-axis chart) can be misleading because the creator can ____ the scales to imply a false correlation between two metrics.

options.text: Independently manipulate
Randomly generate
Permanently lock
Automatically standardize

interactions.prompt: You're presenting Slack adoption data to executives. You have 12 months of daily active users showing steady growth. Do you use a line chart with a y-axis starting at zero (growth looks modest) or start the y-axis at your baseline (growth looks impressive)?

options.text: Start at zero — accuracy builds long-term trust with leadership
Start at baseline — executives need to see the growth clearly
Show both versions side by side for full context
Skip the chart and just show the percentage increase

interactions.prompt: A KPI dashboard at HubSpot shows churn rate dropping from 5.2% to 4.8%. The sparkline chart next to it uses a 3-month moving average. Why use a moving average?

options.text: It makes the number look better for investors
It smooths out short-term noise to reveal the real trend
It hides months where churn increased
It's required by financial reporting standards

interactions.teachingPreamble: KPI dashboards often use smoothing techniques like moving averages to help decision-makers focus on trends rather than reacting to daily or weekly fluctuations. A single bad week might spike a metric, but a 3-month moving average shows whether the overall direction is improving. However, you should always be able to drill into the raw data — smoothing can sometimes mask real problems.

interactions.prompt: You're reviewing an unfamiliar dashboard for the first time. Rank these steps from what you should do first to last to correctly interpret the data.

options.text: Draw conclusions and recommend actions
Check axes, scales, and date ranges on each chart
Identify what KPIs and metrics are being tracked
Look for trends, outliers, and relationships between metrics

interactions.prompt: Your colleague points out the dashboard's revenue chart uses a logarithmic y-axis instead of linear. The growth that looked steady is actually exponential. How does this change your recommendation?

options.text: Logarithmic axes are always wrong — switch to linear immediately
Exponential growth means capacity planning is more urgent than expected
It doesn't matter — the trend direction is the same either way
Ignore the chart and rely only on the raw numbers

interactions.priorContext: Previously you reviewed a KPI dashboard and interpreted revenue as growing steadily. Now you discover the y-axis is logarithmic, meaning equal visual distances represent multiplicative (not additive) changes — steady-looking growth is actually accelerating exponentially.
